claims.evidence: NHS BMI page: cannot tell muscle from fat. Waist size and GP discussion are consistent with the NHS waist and overweight pages.
NHS BMI page: calculator checks whether adult is a healthy weight for height.
BMI page: very muscular adults/athletes may be classed overweight; older adults who lose muscle may look healthy while carrying excess fat.
BMI page: higher chance of health problems at a lower BMI in Black, Asian and some other minority ethnic groups.
Obesity - NHS: lifestyle changes, local programmes, medicines (orlistat, specialist-prescribed) and surgery.
BMI page: BMI calculator checks healthy weight for height in adults.
BMI page: healthy range 18.5 to 23 for Black, Asian and some other minority ethnic groups, 18.5 to 24.9 otherwise.
BMI page: risk of conditions such as type 2 diabetes at a lower BMI.
BMI page: cannot tell the difference between muscle and fat. The 'too much weight rather than too much fat' gloss was not in the returned text.
claims.newSentence: BMI cannot tell the difference between muscle and fat.

claims.evidence: BMI page: very muscular adults and athletes may be classed overweight or obese even though body fat is low.
BMI page: adults who lose muscle with age may appear healthy while carrying excess fat.
NHS 'why is my waist size important' page: midpoint between lowest rib and hip bone, tape snug, breathe out naturally. Instruction-style how-to; kept as a description of the NHS method.

Waist-to-height ratio of 0.5 to 0.59 = increased health risks, 0.6+ further increase (NHS/NICE/BHF). The specific list 'heart disease, type 2 diabetes and stroke' for this ratio is not stated by NHS text found (BHF covers heart/circulatory; diabetes via BHF).
claims.newSentence: The NHS and NICE describe a waist measurement of more than half a person's height as linked with increased health risks.

claims.evidence: 'BMI as a starting point for a GP discussion' was not found in returned text. NHS overweight page does advise seeing a GP for help losing weight or if waist is more than half of height.
claims.newSentence: The NHS advises seeing a GP for help with losing weight, or if the waist measurement is more than half of height.

claims.evidence: No returned text confirmed a GP checking blood pressure, glucose, cholesterol and waist at a BMI discussion; NHS diagnosis text says the GP looks for underlying causes.
Returned NHS text says a GP can advise on safe weight loss and refer to programmes, medicines or surgery; 'it can be hard to lose weight' was not found.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says a GP can advise on weight loss and on options such as weight management programmes, medicines or surgery.

claims.evidence: Obesity - NHS: lifestyle changes, weight management programmes, medicines, surgery.
Not from NHS England or nhsinform: local NHS trust pages (e.g. Addenbrooke's) describe tier 3 teams with consultant, specialist nurses, dietitians, clinical psychologist; composition varies by area.
claims.newSentence: Local NHS specialist weight management services, often called tier 3, usually have a team that can include a doctor, dietitians, specialist nurses and psychologists.

claims.evidence: Outdated/overbroad: tirzepatide (Mounjaro) has been prescribable by GP practices since 23 June 2025 in phased cohorts (ICB pages); Wegovy/Saxenda were NICE-restricted to specialist services in several ICB statements. NHS 111 Wales still says liraglutide/semaglutide via specialist service. england.nhs.uk page appeared in results but its text was not returned.
claims.newSentence: NHS access to weight-loss injections such as semaglutide and tirzepatide depends on eligibility criteria and varies by area; some are offered through specialist weight management services, and tirzepatide is being introduced through GP practices in phases for people with the highest clinical need.

claims.evidence: Returned NHS text lists type 2 diabetes, heart disease, stroke, high blood pressure, several cancers, osteoarthritis, fatty liver disease. Musculoskeletal, infertility and psychiatric were not confirmed (and nhsinform was not returned).
claims.newSentence: The NHS lists type 2 diabetes, heart disease, stroke, high blood pressure, several cancers, osteoarthritis and fatty liver disease among conditions linked to excess weight.

claims.evidence: NHS overweight and obesity page: having more body fat than the body needs.
NHS page: can happen when you eat or drink more than the body needs or do not do enough physical activity.
Returned NHS text: genes, certain medicines, some health conditions such as underactive thyroid. Specific drug classes (steroids, antidepressants, beta blockers) were not seen in returned text.
claims.newSentence: Other factors listed include genes, some medicines, and some health conditions such as an underactive thyroid.

claims.evidence: NHS diagnosis text: GP looks for underlying causes, for example medication being taken. Specific tests list (diabetes blood test, cholesterol, BP) not confirmed.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says a GP looks for possible underlying causes of obesity, for example a medicine the person is taking.

claims.evidence: The NHS weight loss plan is a free 12-week app (NHS-linked pages). 'Downloadable guide' not confirmed.
claims.newSentence: The NHS offers a free 12-week weight loss plan as an app.

claims.evidence: Obesity - NHS (search summary): losing about 3% of body weight and keeping it off can lower risk of obesity-related complications such as diabetes and heart disease. A later search did not re-surface the figure, so moderate confidence.

notes: Search budget ran out. c19 (weight-loss medicines) is the key risk: policy is changing fast; wording is deliberately general. Waist-method sentence (c12) is a how-to; wording describes the NHS method. 3% figure (c26) appeared once only. Ledger URLs for c12/c13, c18, c20 pointed to pages that did not carry the claim (myhealthlondon, nhsinform).
